Ceuta and Melilla have no debt series, so they have no score. The number does not say the president caused it.

pileCaption: Each counted year changes the volume, and the next year starts from that new volume, through the end of the mandate. It is not the average of the years, and the yearly gaps are not added up. If they are still in office, the last year is {year}. The slider is that total against Spain.
exIntro: The percentage is this community's share of Spain's GDP now, divided by its share at the start, minus 1. GDP is production, in units of this example. People sit underneath and stay out of the division.
exBefore: Before. Each has 100 GDP and Spain has 1,000 GDP, so each is 10.00%.
exYear1: Year 1. 10 GDP moves from Madrid to Castilla y León, with the work of 10 people. Spain stays at 1,000 GDP.
exYear2: Year 2. 10 people arrive from another country and produce 10 GDP in Castilla y León. That 10 GDP also enters Spain, which goes to 1,010 GDP.
exYear3: Year 3. 5 GDP goes back to Madrid with 5 people. Spain stays at 1,010 GDP.
exYear4: Year 4. The people stay the same. Castilla y León produces 5 more GDP with the same people. Spain goes to 1,015 GDP.
exFoot: Year 2, Castilla y León: 120 GDP divided by 1,010 GDP is 11.88% of Spain. 11.88 divided by the starting 10.00, minus 1, is +18.8%. If Spain had stayed at 1,000 GDP, 120 divided by 1,000 would be 12.00% and the change +20%. Year 4 splits people from GDP: there are 115 people, and the division uses 120 GDP divided by 1,015 GDP, 11.82%, which gives +18.2%. Madrid stays at 95 GDP: 95 divided by 1,015 is 9.36%, which gives -6.4%. Someone who only changes house and keeps working in Madrid leaves the GDP in Madrid.

asksTitle: What would make the next list fair
ask1Body: One rule for who is on the waiting list, and for how a day is counted. Write it down before the term starts, and keep it for the whole term.
ask2Title: Publish both numbers when the count changes
ask2Body: If a community changes the rule, print the old figure and the new figure for that same month. Without both, a later fall cannot be joined to the earlier list.
ask3Title: Print every December, including the one before they take office
ask3Body: {blank} of {total} ranked presidents have no surgery figure. A comparison needs the December before their first counted year and the December of their last. A list that starts in the middle of a term leaves the cell blank.
ask4Title: Publish surgery and care at the end of every month
ask4Body: A queue should be visible during the term, not only at the next December. The ranking still compares the same month of the year, because August is a slow month for operations. A weekly list follows the rota and gives the hospital a publication day to manage. School leaving and the size of the economy are yearly figures, from a survey and the annual accounts. Debt is counted each quarter.
ask5Title: Show the people behind the percentage
ask5Body: How many applied, how many were recognised, how many received a plan, how many are still waiting, and how many days each step took. A share can fall because fewer people were recognised.
ask6Title: Say who was in charge, and on which days
ask6Body: The day they started and the day they stopped, including acting presidents. Health and schools in Ceuta and Melilla are run by the state. Those two cities are also missing from the debt series. The Basque Country and Navarra collect their own taxes, so their debt is a different obligation.
coverSchools: {from}–{to}. One definition for every community. This is the series that already works.
coverHealth: {from}–{to}. Average days already waited on 31 December. Each community sends its own count.
coverCare: {from}–{to}. A share of people, not a wait in days.
coverDebt: {from}–{to}. The change in the community’s own debt. The debt they inherited stays out of the score. Ceuta and Melilla have no figure, so they are unranked.
coverReal: {from}–{to}. Real output, with local prices taken out. Firms, visitors, and decisions taken in Madrid move it too. It stays on the row so you can see the term.
missingFoot: A dash on the presidents list means that figure was not published for their years. The score still uses the worst change on record, so a blank cell is not left out of the result. Prices, population, and jobs stay on the row so you can see the term. They do not decide the rank.
missingMethod: See how a score is built
dataDeck: Every number on this site comes from a public file. Here is which one, who publishes it, which years, and whether it enters the score.
dataInDeck: Real output adds up each counted year through the end of the mandate. Debt, schools, care, and surgery compare that end with the year before they took office, against Spain.
dataBesideTitle: Shown on the row, and kept out of the score
dataBesideDeck: These figures show the term. The rank does not use them.
dataPeopleDeck: The score belongs to the person who presided over the community. Cabinet members are shown and not scored.
dataList: Open the list this site uses
dataReal: National Statistics Institute. {title}. The volume rates are not rounded to one decimal, and each year multiplies into the next from 2000. The score uses the volume at the end of the mandate against the year before they took office, compared with Spain. From {from} to {to}.
dataDebt: Bank of Spain. {title}. December debt, divided by the community’s own current-price GDP. Half the change during the counted years enters the score. Inherited debt stays out. Ceuta and Melilla are not in this series. From {from} to {to}.
dataSchools: Eurostat. {title}. One definition for the whole country. From {from} to {to}.
dataCare: IMSERSO. {title}. A share of people on 31 December, not a number of days. From {from} to {to}.
dataHealth: Ministry of Health. {title}. Each community sends its own count. Ten days count as one point. Andalucía changed the count in December 2018. From {from} to {to}.
dataGdp: National Statistics Institute, table {table}. {title}. This is the community’s share of Spain, the chart, and the divisor for debt. Population is calculated from it too. From {from} to {to}.
dataPerson: National Statistics Institute, table {table}. {title}. This is the per-person column. It does not enter the score. From {from} to {to}.
dataPop: There is no separate population file. People are current-price GDP divided by GDP per person. The change against Spain is shown and does not enter the score.
dataJobs: National Statistics Institute, table {table}. {title}. Both sexes. The year’s quarters are averaged. The change against Spain is shown and does not enter the score. From {from}.
dataOffice: Names and days come from Wikidata, office P39, and from the Spanish Wikipedia lists when those lists cover {from}–{to}. Hand-corrected dates are kept in a project file. An open mandate is counted through 31 December {to}.
dataBalance: General Comptroller of the State Administration. {title}. Each community’s financing capacity or need, as a share of its GDP. Above zero, it took in more than it spent. The Basque Country and Navarre collect their own taxes. From {from} to {to}.
dataBudget: Ministry of Finance. {title}. What was spent, under the same names in every community. Pensions and repayment of principal stay out. Each spending policy is shown on its own. Interest is the financial chapter of spending. The series starts in 2002 and runs to {to}.
dataStateBudget: General Comptroller of the State Administration. {title}. This is the budget law the Cortes pass each year, once it has been spent. For Spain each spending policy is shown on its own. Transfers inside that budget and repayment of principal stay out. From {from} to {to}.
dataCentral: General Comptroller of the State Administration. {title}. This is central-government spending in the national accounts. It leaves out the communities, town councils, and social security. From {from} to {to}.
dataSpain: General Comptroller of the State Administration. {title}. The surplus or deficit of every public administration together, and also their spending, which is Spain's table. From {from} to {to}.
dataSpainDebt: Bank of Spain. {title}. December debt of every public administration together. The change is how much it rose or fell during the block. Debt / economy divides it by the size of Spain's economy.
dataEu: European Commission. {title}. Received is what the EU budget spends in Spain, plus NextGenerationEU from 2021. Paid back is Spain's contribution to that budget, including customs duties when the table lists them apart. From 2000 to 2025.
dataEuVolumeTitle: Real growth of the European Union
dataEuVolume: Eurostat, table nama_10_gdp. {title}. This is the real volume of gross domestic product. The European Union is the present one of 27 countries. In Spain's table, growth against Spain compares Spain's volume with the Union's, in the same way a community is compared with Spain. From {from} to {to}.
dataFlow: Ministry of Finance. {title}. Chapters 40 and 70 of the settled revenue and spending. A positive line is money the state transfers to the community. A negative line is money the community pays into the system. The town councils' share of state taxes stays out. The series starts in 2002 and runs to {to}.
commDeck: Spain is the table above, for the chosen block. Below, each community is in that same block. Real growth is that row's own. Against Spain is that same growth compared with the country's. In Spain's table that comparison is with the European Union's real growth.
commNote: A law voted in the block is a dot on the year of the vote. The dot is the vote. The line after it is the economy.
commGrowth: The community's real growth in these years
commGrowthSpain: Spain's real growth in these years
commDuring: Real growth against Spain in these years
commDuringEu: Real growth against the EU in these years
commLaterGrowth: The community's real growth in the next four years
commLaterGrowthSpain: Spain's real growth in the next four years
commLater: Real growth against Spain in the next four years
commLaterEu: Real growth against the EU in the next four years
commBalanceEnd: Surplus or deficit at the end
commScaleNote: The economy, the debt at the end, spending, and the surplus or deficit at the end are the last year of the block, in millions of euros. Change in debt is how much that debt rose or fell during the block. Debt / economy is what the government owed, divided by what the community produced that year. Change in debt / economy is how many points that percentage rose or fell since the end of the previous block. Surplus or deficit says whether that government took in more than it spent during the block, as a share of the economy. In Spain's table, the debt and the spending of every public administration are the whole. Central government spending is the central administration alone, in those same accounts.
commFlowNote: Received from the state and paid back to the state add up the years of the block, in millions of euros, from the settled budget. Received is what the state transfers to the community, without the part that only passes through to town councils. Paid back is what the community contributes when a financing-system line is negative, plus what the budget pays the state. It is not the taxes inhabitants pay, and it is not pensions. The Basque Country and Navarre use another system: they collect their own taxes, and these columns are the lines their settled budget records with the state. In Spain's table, received and paid back are with the European Union: what the EU budget spends in Spain, plus NextGenerationEU when it exists, and what Spain contributes to that budget. The difference with the EU is what was paid back minus what was received: above zero, Spain contributed more. Paid to the communities and received from the communities add up what each community records with the state. The difference with the communities is what was received minus what was paid: below zero, the state paid more.
commScaleLine: At the end of {year}, the economy was {gdp}.
commScaleDebt: The government owed {debt}, {share} of that economy.
commChart: Real production against Spain. 100 is the same level as Spain in 2000.
commChartEu: Real production against the European Union. 100 is the same level as the European Union in 2000.
commLawsEmpty: This community has no laws in the register yet.
commBudgetPartsSpain: The smaller bars are the pieces of the bar above them, on the same scale. The Royal Household, Parliament, the Constitutional Court and the Court of Auditors sit inside Government and constitutional bodies. The courts and prosecutors sit inside Justice. Embassies and consulates sit inside Foreign policy.
commBudgetParts: The smaller bars split general services into staff, supplies, transfers, investment and financial assets. This liquidation does not separate the parliament, the courts or offices abroad.
commBudgetHelp: What was spent, without pensions and without repayment of principal. Each bar is one spending policy. Interest is the financial chapter of spending. The figure above is that spending against GDP in the same years.
commBudgetHelpSpain: Liquidation of the State budget, the law the Cortes pass each year. Each bar is one spending policy of that budget. Interest is the financial chapter of spending. Pensions are the pensions policy, mostly civil-service pensions. Transfers inside that budget and repayment of principal stay out: the public-debt policy is that interest plus that principal. Transport includes transport subsidies, roads and rail; the rest of the infrastructure-and-ecosystems policy has its own bar. It is not the spending of every administration, and it is not the contributory pensions paid by social security. The figure above is that spending against GDP in the same years.
commBudgetMissing: This block has no settled budget.
commBudgetPartial: The settled figures in this block cover {span}.
commBalanceHelp: National-accounts financing capacity or need. The percent is the whole block, weighted by the size of the economy each year, as a share of GDP. Above zero, the government took in more than it spent. The figure in millions is the last year only.
commForal: This community collects its own taxes.
commSpain: This page is the whole country. Real growth is the reference for the other communities. Against Spain is Spain's real growth compared with the European Union's. The surplus or deficit, the debt and the spending of every public administration are the whole. Central government spending is the central administration alone. The settled budget is the State's, the law the Cortes pass each year. Received and paid back are with the European Union, and their difference is what was paid back minus what was received. Paid to the communities and received from them add up what they record with the state. The difference with the communities is what was received minus what was paid.
commFlowHelp: Sum of the block's years that have a settled budget, in millions of euros. Received is what the state transfers to this community, without the part that only passes through to town councils. Paid back is what it contributes when a financing-system line is negative, plus what the budget pays the state. It is not the taxes inhabitants pay, and it is not pensions.
commFlowHelpEu: Sum of the years of the block, in millions of euros. Received is what the EU budget spends in Spain, and from 2021 also NextGenerationEU. Paid back is what Spain contributes to that budget. When the table lists customs duties apart, they are included in what is paid back. The difference is what was paid back minus what was received: above zero, Spain contributed more.
commScaleDebtSpain: Every public administration together owed {debt}, {share} of that economy.
commBurdenChangeLine: Since the end of the previous block, debt / economy changed {change}.
commScaleSpentSpain: Spending by every public administration together was {spent}.
commStateHelp: Sum of the block's years that have a settled budget, in millions of euros. Paid to the communities is what they record as received from the state. Received from the communities is what they record as paid back to the state. The difference is what was received minus what was paid: below zero, the state paid more. Each community with a settled budget for that year is included.
commDebtHelp: The change is how much more, or less, was owed between the December before the block and the December at the end. Beside it, how much of the stock is bonds and how much is loans.
commNoDebt: This community has no debt figure.
commFund: Of the loans, {n} come from the state financing fund.
commBlockSoon: The next four years are not finished yet.
